name: Siklos Waves and the Kaigorodov Spacetime
description: Exact gravitational waves crossing anti-de Sitter space: a pp-wave multiplied by anti-de Sitter's conformal factor, with fronts that are hyperbolic planes. The simplest, Kaigorodov's spacetime, is homogeneous, and its singularity shows in no curvature scalar.
convention: The anti-de Sitter radius $L$ is a length, with $\Lambda = -3/L^2$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: What does a gravitational wave look like in a universe curved everywhere? The textbook waves, the pp-waves that Heinrich Brinkmann met in 1925, cross flat space on plane fronts [brinkmann1925, ehlerskundt1962]. Anti-de Sitter space has no flat space to offer, since its negative cosmological constant $\Lambda$ curves it equally at every point [hawking1973]. Stephen Siklos wrote down the waves that cross it in 1985, $$ds^2 = \frac{L^2}{x^2}\left(dx^2 + dy^2 - 2\,du\,dv + H\,du^2\right),$$ with $L = \sqrt{-3/\Lambda}$ [siklos1985, podolsky1998]. The bracket is a pp-wave of profile $H(u, x, y)$, the factor in front is anti-de Sitter's, and at $H = 0$ only anti-de Sitter space is left [podolsky1998].¶Einstein's equations with $\Lambda$ ask one thing of the profile, $$\partial_x^2 H + \partial_y^2 H - \frac{2}{x}\,\partial_x H = 0,$$ and $u$ never enters, so any solution may be switched on and off along $u$ as you please [podolsky1998]. A surface of constant $u$ and $v$ is a wave front, and here it is the hyperbolic plane, which is why Siklos called his solutions "Lobatchevski plane gravitational waves" [siklos1985, podolsky1998]. They are also the only ones of their kind: no other solution with a cosmological constant is a curved pp-wave multiplied by a function of position [podolsky1998, bicak1999]. István Ozsváth, Ivor Robinson, and Krzysztof Rózga reached the same family that year by giving the plane-fronted waves a cosmological constant [ozsvath1985, podolsky1998]. The name Siklos waves came in 2006 from Piotr Chruściel, Daniel Maerten, and Paul Tod, "which we propose to call Siklos waves" [chrusciel2006rigid].¶The simplest of them was twenty three years old by then [kaigorodov1962, podolsky1998]. It sits in a paper of 1962 by Vladimir Kaigorodov of Kazan on Einstein spaces "of maximum mobility", and in Siklos's coordinates it is the profile $H = x^3/L^3$ [kaigorodov1962, podolsky1998]. His spacetime is homogeneous, one event like any other, with five independent symmetries where anti-de Sitter space has ten [podolsky1998, cvetic1999]. It is of type N in Aleksei Petrov's classification, the type of a pure gravitational wave, and no other vacuum of that type with a cosmological constant is homogeneous [petrov1954, podolsky1998]. Jiří Podolský took it for the counterpart in anti-de Sitter space of the homogeneous plane wave in flat space [podolsky1998].¶Are these really waves? Podolský's answer of 1998 was to follow free particles [podolsky1998]. The neighbours of any one particle feel two things: the pull of anti-de Sitter space, the same in every direction, and a squeeze and stretch across the direction of travel, in the two polarisations of a gravitational wave [podolsky1998]. The squeeze and stretch vanish exactly when the space is anti-de Sitter's [podolsky1998]. Seen from a frame that a falling particle carries along without turning, the wave's direction of travel rotates at the angular velocity $c/L$, which Podolský found "somewhat surprising" [podolsky1998].¶Where does Kaigorodov's wave end? At $x = 0$ it has an infinity like anti-de Sitter's, which no falling particle reaches [podolsky1998]. At $x = \infty$ falling observers arrive in a finite time by their own clocks, and the wave's amplitude on them grows along the way as $x^5$ [podolsky1998]. Every scalar built from the curvature is constant, so none of them shows the singularity [cvetic1999, chamblin2000supergravity]. It is a pp curvature singularity, where the curvature diverges in a falling observer's own frame [chamblin2000supergravity, brecher2001].¶Mirjam Cvetič, Hong Lü, and Christopher Pope ran into Kaigorodov's metric in 1998, next to a stack of membranes [cvetic1999]. Close to M2 branes at rest the geometry is anti-de Sitter space times a sphere of seven dimensions, and with a wave running along the branes it is Kaigorodov's spacetime times that sphere [cvetic1999]. They read it as anti-de Sitter space boosted to the speed of light, and conjectured that it describes a conformal field theory in the infinite momentum frame with a constant density of momentum [cvetic1999]. Dominic Brecher, Andrew Chamblin, and Harvey Reall computed that density from the metric and found it constant [brecher2001]. Chamblin and Gary Gibbons had by then put Siklos's waves on the brane world of Lisa Randall and Raman Sundrum, where the singularities lie "where the horizon of AdS would ordinarily be" [chamblin2000supergravity].

related.text: The wave switched off. At $H = 0$ the metric is anti-de Sitter space in the coordinates of its Poincaré patch [podolsky1998].
The cosmological constant switched off. In the coordinates of Ozsváth, Robinson, and Rózga, $1/L = 0$ leaves a pp-wave in Brinkmann's form [ozsvath1985, podolsky1998].

The field of a massless particle in flat space, a pp-wave squeezed onto one front. Squeeze a Siklos wave the same way and it is the field of a null particle in anti-de Sitter space [podolsky1998impulsive].

Gravitational waves of the same algebraic type on fronts that expand. With a cosmological constant, a wave of type N without twist is either one of Kundt's, as Siklos's are, or one of Robinson and Trautman's [bicak1999].
In three dimensions Kaigorodov's metric is the extreme BTZ black hole, the one spinning as fast as its mass allows [cvetic1999].
A wave of this form in five dimensions, rolled up along its null direction, is Lifshitz spacetime at $z = 2$, where time scales as the square of space [balasubramanian2010, donos2010].
Siklos's line element at the profile $H = -\beta^2/x^2$, which fails his vacuum equation and so needs matter. Its symmetries are those of the free Schrödinger equation [son2008, duval2009].

The wider family of Ozsváth, Robinson, and Rózga, sorted by the sign of one invariant. Siklos's waves are the case where it vanishes, and where it is positive the fronts roll round an envelope, as the fronts of Kundt's waves do [ozsvath1985, bicak1999, griffiths2004].

coordinates.name: Siklos

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -3/L^2$

Wave profile, a dimensionless function of $u$ and of the two coordinates along the wave front. The metric solves Einstein's equations with $\Lambda = -3/L^2$ and no matter exactly where $\partial_x^2 H + \partial_y^2 H - (2/x)\,\partial_x H = 0$; $H = 0$ is anti-de Sitter space, and so is $H = c_0 + c_1y + c_2(x^2 + y^2)$ for any functions $c_0$, $c_1$, and $c_2$ of $u$

coordinates.convention: We use Siklos's coordinates $(u, v, x, y)$, all lengths, with $u$ labelling the wave fronts and $v$ an affine parameter along the rays. We leave the profile $H$ free, so no component assumes a field equation. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Ozsváth-Robinson-Rózga
domains: \xi^2 + \eta^2 < 4L^2 \;\text{(the disc; its rim is the conformal boundary)}

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -3/L^2$; at $1/L = 0$ the metric is a pp-wave in Brinkmann's form

Wave profile of this chart, a dimensionless function of $u$, $\xi$, and $\eta$, equal to $LH/x$ for the $H$ and $x$ of Siklos's chart. The metric solves Einstein's equations with $\Lambda = -3/L^2$ and no matter exactly where $p^2(\partial_\xi^2 h + \partial_\eta^2 h) = 2h/L^2$, and Kaigorodov's spacetime is $h = p^2/q^2$
Conformal factor of the wave front, the hyperbolic plane drawn as Poincaré's disc of radius $2L$
The second function of Ozsváth, Robinson, and Rózga, with $q/p = L/x$ for the $x$ of Siklos's chart

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates of Ozsváth, Robinson, and Rózga, all lengths: $u$ and $v$ are Siklos's, and $\xi + i\eta = 2L(L - x - iy)/(L + x + iy)$ maps his half plane onto the disc $\xi^2 + \eta^2 < 4L^2$. We leave the profile $h$ free, so no component assumes a field equation. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Kaigorodov, Siklos Coordinates

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -3/L^2$; the curvature singularity is $x \to \infty$ and the conformal boundary is $x \to 0$

coordinates.convention: We use Siklos's coordinates $(u, v, x, y)$, all lengths, with the profile $H = x^3/L^3$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Kaigorodov, Poincaré

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -3/L^2$; the conformal boundary is $z \to 0$, as in the Poincaré patch of anti-de Sitter space

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ lengths; the wave travels along $x$, and $z$ is the $x$ of Siklos's chart, whose null coordinates are $u = (ct - x)/\sqrt{2}$ and $v = (ct + x)/\sqrt{2}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Kaigorodov, Horospheric

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -3/L^2$; the conformal boundary is $\rho \to \infty$ and the curvature singularity $\rho \to -\infty$

coordinates.convention: We use Kaigorodov's coordinates $(u, v, y, \rho)$, all lengths, with $\rho = -L\ln(x/L)$ the proper distance across the surfaces of constant $x$ of Siklos's chart. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Kaigorodov, Stationary Region

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -3/L^2$; the conformal boundary is $\rho \to \infty$

coordinates.convention: We use Kaigorodov's coordinates $(u, v, y, \rho)$, all lengths, on the region $x < 0$ of Siklos's chart, with $\rho = -L\ln(-x/L)$; there $\partial_u$ is timelike. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Kaigorodov, Homogeneous Form

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -3/L^2$
A positive number of no physical meaning; rescaling $X$ and $U$ changes it

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(U, X, y, Z)$, with $U$, $X$, and $y$ lengths and $Z$ a pure number: $x = Le^{2Z}$, $u = -\sqrt{10k}\,X$, and $v = -Ue^{5Z}/\sqrt{10k}$ in Siklos's coordinates. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Kaigorodov, Kundt Form

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -3/L^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(U, V, x, y)$, with $U$ and $V$ lengths and $x$ and $y$ pure numbers, $L$ times which are Siklos's $x$ and $y$; his null coordinates are $u = \sqrt{2}\,U$ and $v = Vx^2/\sqrt{2}$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
